title: 21. Friday and the Two Festivals
purpose: It compiles the legal rulings and the esoteric interpretations governing the Friday prayer and the prayers of the two festivals, drawing on the question-and-answer collection and the doctrinal sources.

points.text: The compiler reports the ruling that Friday prayer is established in two congregational mosques only if three miles or more separate them, and that if the distance is less than three miles it is established in only one, whether the mosques stand in one city or in two.

Against al-Muayyad's sermon wording that abandoning Friday prayer is blameworthy 'whether under a just imam or an unjust one', the answer given is that praying behind the people of injustice is permissible only for the sake of dissimulation (taqiyyah).

Support for this is drawn from al-Baqir Muhammad ibn Ali, who instructed that prayer behind a nasib or haruri not be counted, and that such a leader be treated as a pillar of the mosque while one recites for oneself as if praying alone.

Al-Husayn ibn Ali is reported to have put Muawiya's governor forward to lead the prayer over al-Hasan, saying 'were it not for the practice I would not have put you forward', which the compiler explains as the practice of the People of the House in dissimulation, one Imam having said 'dissimulation is my religion and the religion of my fathers'.

A distinction is drawn: 'the unjust' in the sermon means one appointed among the summoners in whom injustice has appeared — behind him prayer is still obligatory, but the people must bring the matter before the holder of authority and await his response.

Mukhtasar al-Musannaf is cited for rulings of precedence and procedure: prayer behind the Imam of the Muslims excels prayer behind his deputies; the binding call is the one given before the seated preacher; a sale then made is not annulled; and detailed remedies are given for broken purity, omitted sitting between sermons, and congregations that disperse mid-prayer.

Tawil al-Shariah states that the sermon precedes the prayer, the prayer is two cycles, the sermon is divided by a sitting, the raised voice distinguishes it from the ordinary noon prayer, and the call to stand comes after the sermon.

Tawil al-Shariah further equates the conduct of respondents in the assembly of the summoner with that of the Friday congregation: silence and listening are obligatory, and the respondent may not press proposals or demand branches of knowledge from the summoner, who knows better how to raise his children.

Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl's Hidden Epistle interprets the Friday prayer as pointing to Muhammad, gate of the Garden, possessor of an outward summons to his Shariah and an inward summons to its interpretation; the reduction to two cycles with the sermon substituting for the other two, and the sitting as the separation between the upper and lower lights with which the Qaim rises.

Ali ibn Abi Talib's Four Hundred Points of Conduct names three hours for seeking a need from God: Friday at the sun's zenith, when the winds blow and the gates of heaven open, and the last hour of night at dawn, when two angels call out for the repentant, the asker, and the seeker of forgiveness.

On the festivals, 'tashriq' is glossed as the prayer of the two festivals, so named because it is prayed at sunrise and its performer is called al-mushriq, and it is not incumbent on the traveler except in a congregational city.

The twenty-three magnifications from Arafah to the last day of tashriq are interpreted as a likeness of the summons of the five speakers of firm resolve corresponding to the five prayers, drawn from the ten spiritual and ten bodily ranks plus the speaker of the cycle, his executor, and the Imam of the age — the local addition of a twenty-fourth being noted as a departure.

Festival practice is specified: a congregation of five including the Imam as with Friday; the washing is a prophetic practice from dawn to the sun's zenith; hands are raised at every magnification; the festival prayer is not prayed in congregation at Mina but individually, as verified from Idris ibn Hasan.

Zayd ibn Muhammad ibn al-Fadl derives al-fitr from senses of splitting open, appearing and beginning, so that fasting is silence and concealment — evidenced by Maryam's vow of a fast of silence — and the day of breaking the fast is the day secrets and hidden knowledge are manifested.

He adds that the festival prayer has neither call to prayer nor call to stand, that the breaking-of-the-fast sermon uniquely follows the prayer as a sign that the command appears otherwise than in past cycles, and that every sermon opens with praise except the sermon of the day of sacrifice, which opens with four magnifications.
entities: festival of the breaking of the fast
